newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries close lower as retail sales due. [CORRECTED 00:41 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries close lower as retail sales due. [CORRECTED 00:41 GMT]

text.p: The prices of U.S. Treasury securities closed lower on Tuesday after a fairly volatile trading session that reflected nervousness ahead of July retail sales data due Wednesday.
A surprising retail sales number could jolt the market, according to economists who called retail sales the primary release of a week in which a number of economic releases were expected.
Data were expected to show retail sales rose 0.7 percent -- 0.5 percent excluding automobiles -- in July.
"We had some selling pressure at the long end of the market and the Redbook report showed strength," said Kathleen Stephansen, senior economist with Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp.
The Redbook report was up by 0.9 percent in the first week of August with most retailers saying sales were better than planned.
Stephansen saw retail sales rising by 0.7 percent, and 0.5 percent excluding autos. The Federal Reserve can remain on the sidelines in August, she said.
"The market had priced in the best of all worlds," she said, but would now have to pause to see if economic growth was slowing to a sustainable level.
Price movement this session had very little to do with the fundamental economy, said David Orr, chief capital markets economist at First Union Corp.
"Traders got overly optimistic after Greenspan's (Humphrey Hawkins testimony)," he said. "They were now trying to resell last week's auction."
Despite what were seen as decent results at last week's Treasury refunding, dealers said much remained to be absorbed.

Orr said that in the new view of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, strong growth was not necessarily a reason to raise official interest rates as long as productivity remained high and inflation low.
The U.S. economy slowed in the second quarter following growth the Fed saw as unsustainable in the first quarter. Many economists feared growth would pick up again in the second half of 1997.
The Treasury's 30-year issue ended down (corrects direction of movement from up) 15/32 at 96-3/32 to yield 6.68 percent.

At the short end of the maturity spectrum, three-month bills were one basis point higher at 5.18 percent. Six-month bills were up one basis point at 5.24 percent and year bills were up one basis point at 5.33 percent.
The 10-year issue was off 9/32 at 97-30/32 to yield 6.41 percent. The five-year was 5/32 lower at 99-even to yield 6.24 percent and the two-year 2/32 lower to yield 6.01 percent.
